The Persistence of Small Joys

There is a particular quality to the light that filters through the kitchen window at approximately 3:47 on a Tuesday afternoon in late October. I have become something of an amateur chronicler of this phenomenon, though I possess no scientific instruments beyond my own unreliable memory and the notebook I keep in the drawer beneath the cutting board. The light at this hour, when the sun has begun its descent but has not yet committed to the golden theatrics of true evening, falls across the worn wooden table in a way that makes the dust motes visible—not dramatically, not like a stage effect, but as a quiet population going about their invisible business suddenly made briefly, accidentally seen.

I think often about visibility and its relationship to meaning. We are taught to seek the grand gesture, the mountaintop experience, the transformative moment that cleaves life into a clear before and after. But I have grown suspicious of such narratives, not because they are false exactly, but because they are incomplete in a way that serves the storyteller more than the truth. The mountaintop, after all, is only visible because of the valley, and most of us spend our hours in the valley, learning the names of plants we never thought to notice, discovering that the creek bed changes its course by imperceptible degrees across decades, coming to understand that the valley has its own ecology, its own dignity, its own light at 3:47 on a Tuesday afternoon.

I knew a woman once who collected stones. Not precious stones—she had no interest in gems or geodes or the polished products of rock tumblers. She collected ordinary stones from ordinary places: the parking lot of a grocery store in Dayton, Ohio; the shoulder of a highway in rural New Mexico; the garden bed of a rental house she occupied for only eleven months in her twenties. Each stone was labeled with date and location, stored in cardboard boxes that filled her closet and eventually her second bedroom. When I asked her about this practice, she told me that the stones were a way of keeping time, of insisting that her presence in these unremarkable places had mattered, that she had been there, that the particular angle of her foot against the particular gravel of that parking lot had been real and singular and worth recording.

I did not understand her then. I was young and hungry for narrative arc, for the dramatic confrontation, for the stone that would be not a stone but a metaphor, a symbol, a turning point. I wanted her collection to mean something I could easily translate, to be about grief or memory or the American road or the fragmentation of modern life. She refused these readings with a gentle stubbornness. They were just stones, she said. They were just places she had been. The meaning, if there was any, was in the accumulation, in the sheer fact of persistence, in the boxes growing heavier each year, in the physical weight of having lived.

I have been thinking about her lately, about the way we carry our lives forward. I am no longer young, though I am not yet old enough to claim the authority of age. I occupy a middle space that feels less like a plateau and more like a long hallway with many doors, some of which I have opened and some of which I have walked past, and some of which I opened once and then closed again, unable to bear what I found inside or perhaps what I failed to find. The hallway is not well-lit. I have learned to navigate it by touch, by the memory of where I have been, by the faint glow that seeps under certain doors at certain hours.

The light at 3:47. I am trying to describe it properly. It is not golden, not yet. It is not the light of revelation. It is a grayish light, frankly, filtered through clouds that have settled in for the afternoon without any particular storm in mind. It makes the room look slightly faded, as though the world has been washed too many times. And yet there is something in this light that I have come to wait for, to anticipate in a way that surprises me. It is the light of the ordinary persisting. It is the light of the kitchen table with its water rings and its small pile of unread mail and the bowl of apples that are just beginning to soften. It is the light of the dust motes, visible, ordinary, briefly glorious in their small dance before the angle shifts and they disappear again into the general atmosphere.

I have been reading about mycelium, the underground networks that connect trees in a forest, that allow them to communicate, to share nutrients, to warn each other of pests. The mycelium is invisible to us, walking through the woods. We see only the mushroom when it fruits, the brief above-ground manifestation of a vast hidden life. But the mushroom is not the point. The mushroom is only the occasional visible moment of a continuous process, the way a sigh might be the only audible evidence of a long held breath. I think about this network when I consider the small joys, the ordinary stones, the particular light. We are trained to value the mushroom, the dramatic fruiting body, the moment that can be photographed and shared and narrated. But the life is in the network, in the persistent connection, in the ongoing work of being present that produces no visible evidence most of the time.

The woman with the stones died last year. I learned of it from a mutual acquaintance, someone who had known her in the final years when I had lost touch. The acquaintance told me that the stones had been distributed, box by box, to friends and relatives who were mostly baffled by the inheritance. What were they supposed to do with a labeled stone from a parking lot in Dayton? I felt a sharp grief when I heard this, not because the stones were destroyed or discarded—I do not know their fate—but because I had failed to understand her when I had the chance. I had wanted her collection to be something other than what it was. I had wanted it to resolve into meaning, to become a story with a point, when perhaps the point was only ever the collection itself, the weight of it, the physical fact of a life lived in specific places at specific times.

I have begun my own collection, though I am not systematic enough to label and box. I collect instead the moments of unremarkable light, the conversations that go nowhere in particular, the feeling of warm water on my hands when I wash the dishes in the evening. I am trying to learn the patience of the mycelium, the persistence of the dust motes, the stubborn materiality of the stone. I am trying to believe that a life can be made of such things, that the accumulation of ordinary presence might be enough, might be more than enough, might be the only thing that was ever real.

The light is shifting now. It is after 4, and the sun has begun its descent in earnest, and the kitchen is taking on the golden tones I once thought were the only ones worth watching for. It is beautiful, this evening light. I do not deny its beauty. But I am learning to love also the light that came before, the gray persistence of the afternoon, the moment when nothing seemed to be happening and yet everything was continuing, underground, invisible, real as a stone in the palm of a hand, warm from having been carried in a pocket across years of ordinary walking through ordinary places, heading nowhere in particular, arriving exactly where we are.
